---REDU.MD---
---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/hasura/graphql-engine
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: hasura/graphql-engine:v2.50.0
  port: 8080
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2", db_extensions ["pgcrypto"])
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: hasura
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ THIS REPO HOLDS TWO DIFFERENT PRODUCTS AND YOU WANT v2. README.md:18 says the code in the \"v3\" folder is the engine that powers Hasura DDN, which is a hosted control plane with its own metadata build pipeline and connector processes; README.md:25-31 says v2 is the current stable Hasura GraphQL Engine. This entry deploys v2, one container, pinned to hasura/graphql-engine:v2.50.0 (on Docker Hub, updated 2026-08-05, matching the v2.50.0 GitHub release). Do not substitute a v3 image, and do not assume a v3 tutorial's variable names apply: they do not. Also note the tag list carries .ubuntu, .ubi, .cli-migrations-v2 and .cli-migrations-v3 variants of the SAME version. Those are different images with different contents, not aliases; the plain tag is the one this recipe means."
  - "⛔⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: HASURA HAS NO USER ACCOUNTS, NO SIGNUP FORM AND NO INSTALL WIZARD. There is nothing to claim and no first-visitor race. Administration is a single shared secret that YOU set at deploy time, HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET, and whoever holds it is the administrator from the first second the process starts. That is the deploy-time shape, which is the safe one by construction, but ONLY IF YOU ACTUALLY SET IT. Verified in Serve.hs:382-388: the variable's default is nothing. Verified in Auth.hs:145-159 and :283: with no admin secret, no auth webhook and no JWT config, the engine resolves to AMNoAuth and maps EVERY request, including an anonymous one from the internet, to the ADMIN role. On a public *.redu.cloud hostname that is: read and write on every table, the full metadata API, and a database dump endpoint. Generate a long alphanumeric secret, pass it in the deploy env, and never deploy this app without one."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH ONCE THE SECRET IS SET, so you can tell a real leak from a normal response. GET /healthz and GET /hasura/healthz answer 200 with the literal text OK (or WARN when metadata is inconsistent), and GET /v1/version answers a JSON version, both without the header, by design: ServerApp.hs:976-985 registers them outside the authenticated handler. GET / redirects to /console and the console HTML shell loads for anyone (ServerApp.hs:1209-1214), but it then asks for the admin secret and every API call it makes carries that header. Everything else, /v1/graphql, /v1/metadata, /v2/query and the pg_dump endpoint, answers 401 with \"x-hasura-admin-secret required, but not found\" (Auth.hs:288-294). If an anonymous /v1/graphql POST ever returns 200, the secret is not in effect. The script in the body of this file proves exactly that, in both directions."
  - "⛔ NEVER SET HASURA_GRAPHQL_UNAUTHORIZED_ROLE ON A PUBLIC INSTANCE UNLESS THAT IS THE PRODUCT. It exists (Serve.hs:493-500) so a request WITHOUT the admin secret gets a named role instead of a 401. That is the correct way to publish a genuinely public read-only API, and it is also the fastest way to open one by accident. Leave it unset unless the user has asked for public access, has defined that role's row and column permissions first, and understands that everything that role can see is world-readable."
  - "⛔ TRIM HASURA_GRAPHQL_ENABLED_APIS. Its default is metadata, graphql, PGDUMP and config (Serve.hs:733-740), and ServerApp.hs:1061 gates POST /v1alpha1/pg_dump on that flag alone. So a database-dump endpoint is on by default; with the admin secret set it needs the header, and with the secret missing it is an anonymous full dump of the user's data over HTTPS. Set HASURA_GRAPHQL_ENABLED_APIS=graphql,metadata,config unless the user actually runs Hasura CLI migrations that need pg_dump. Keep metadata in that list: ServerApp.hs:1210 only serves the console when the console AND the metadata API are both enabled, so dropping metadata silently takes the console with it."
  - "⛔ PRE-CREATE THE pgcrypto EXTENSION OR THE FIRST BOOT FAILS. This is the one that would otherwise cost you the deploy. MonadTx.hs:224-285: Hasura's catalog initialisation runs CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgcrypto, but only when it is not already created, and on SQLSTATE 42501 it aborts with \"pgcrypto extension is required, but the current user doesn't have permission to create it. Please grant superuser permission\". Nothing about that message looks like a Hasura problem, and the container simply does not come up. redu solves it at provision time: pass db_extensions: [\"pgcrypto\"] to deploy_compose and the DB VM runs CREATE EXTENSION as the postgres superuser before your app ever connects (redu-webservice pgExtensions.ts:86-88), which makes Hasura's already-created branch true and the privilege question moot. db_superuser: true also works and is a bigger hammer than this needs."
  - "DATABASE: SET HASURA_GRAPHQL_DATABASE_URL AND NOTHING ELSE, AND KNOW WHAT THAT ONE VARIABLE DOES. App.hs:307-321: given only a database url, that database both STORES THE METADATA and is registered as the default GraphQL source. Given a metadata url as well, the two split. Given NEITHER, the process exits with \"Fatal Error: Either of --metadata-database-url or --database-url option expected\". So, unusually for this library, there is NO silent embedded-database fallback to fall into: Hasura either has a Postgres or it refuses to run. deploy_compose with database:'managed' appends DATABASE_URL as a postgresql:// URL to the project .env, so the compose only has to interpolate it: HASURA_GRAPHQL_DATABASE_URL: ${DATABASE_URL}. Remember deploy_compose APPENDS to the .env and never edits your compose, so the compose must do that interpolation itself."
  - "ONE MANAGED POSTGRES IS ENOUGH HERE, AND THAT IS NOT LUCK. redu's managed Postgres serves exactly ONE database: databaseController.ts:167 creates it with the app user as OWNER and :170,177 write pg_hba lines for that database and `postgres` only, so any second database on the same server is refused at authentication with SQLSTATE 28000 and being superuser does not help. Hasura is fine on one because initialise.sql:14-40 puts every metadata object in the `hdb_catalog` SCHEMA, alongside the user's own tables in `public`, in the same database. Do not split the metadata onto a second managed database \"for cleanliness\": it costs another GBP 0.0174/hr and buys nothing here."
  - "⛔ THE THING A REDEPLOY DESTROYS IS THE METADATA, AND IT IS NOT A KEY, IT IS THE DATABASE URL. Hasura has no encryption key and nothing on disk to lose: tracked tables, relationships, every permission rule, event triggers, cron triggers, remote schemas and actions all live as rows in `hdb_catalog` in the Postgres you pointed it at. Point a redeploy at a DIFFERENT database, or let redu provision a fresh one, and the engine comes up perfectly healthy serving an EMPTY GraphQL schema, with no error anywhere, while every permission rule you wrote is still sitting in the old database. So on every redeploy reuse the SAME managed database, and keep HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET identical too, since every client, CLI config and CI job holds that value. PROVE THE WIRING TOOK, in both directions, because absence alone is not evidence: run `sudo docker exec <container> printenv HASURA_GRAPHQL_DATABASE_URL` and confirm the host in it is the private IP of your managed DB (the positive half, which is also what tells you your exec command worked at all), THEN query the DB and confirm `select count(*) from hdb_catalog.hdb_metadata` returns a row. If the first command errors, the second one's result means nothing."
  - "DELETE BOTH EXTRA SERVICES FROM THE UPSTREAM MANIFEST, AND START FROM THE RIGHT FILE. install-manifests/docker-compose/docker-compose.yaml is the real one. The repo-root docker-compose.yaml is a TEST HARNESS: citus, cockroach, sqlserver and two data-connector agents, and no graphql-engine service at all. From the install manifest, delete the bundled `postgres:15` service (it ships a hardcoded password and you are using a managed database on its own private VM) and delete `data-connector-agent`, a JVM process that exists only to reach Athena, MariaDB, MySQL, Oracle and Snowflake. When you delete the agent you MUST also delete the `depends_on` block that names it, or compose refuses to start at all, and the HASURA_GRAPHQL_METADATA_DEFAULTS value, which is one long JSON string of URIs pointing at that now absent host."
  - "TURN OFF THE TWO THINGS THE UPSTREAM MANIFEST TURNS ON FOR CONVENIENCE. HASURA_GRAPHQL_DEV_MODE defaults to disabled (Serve.hs:902-908) and the manifest sets it to true with its own comment saying it is recommended to disable this in production; dev mode adds internal error detail, including SQL, to API responses. HASURA_GRAPHQL_ENABLE_TELEMETRY defaults to ENABLED (Serve.hs:606-613) and is anonymous usage reporting from both the server and the console: set it to false for an EU-hosted deployment unless the user says otherwise. Also narrow HASURA_GRAPHQL_CORS_DOMAIN: its default is allow-all (Serve.hs:524-531), so set it to the instance's own https origin once you know the hostname."
  - "THE CONSOLE IS ON PURPOSE, BUT SET ITS ASSETS DIR. HASURA_GRAPHQL_ENABLE_CONSOLE defaults to DISABLED (Serve.hs:550-556); this recipe enables it, because a GraphQL API with no console is very hard to get started with, and because with the admin secret set the console is gated behind that secret. Also set HASURA_GRAPHQL_CONSOLE_ASSETS_DIR=/srv/console-assets: the help text at Serve.hs:568-576 says exactly that path on the default docker image stops the console pulling its JavaScript from a CDN, and packaging/graphql-engine/Dockerfile copies rootfs/srv/ to /srv/ so it is there. Serving the console from the instance itself is faster, works from a restricted network, and keeps an EU-hosted deployment honest. If the user wants no console at all, set the enable flag to false and they lose nothing but the UI."
  - "PORT 8080, from HASURA_GRAPHQL_SERVER_PORT's default (Serve.hs:206-212), and the install manifest publishes 8080:8080. Pass 8080 to deploy_compose. Health probe: GET /healthz, which answers the literal text OK, or WARN when metadata is inconsistent, or 500 in strict mode. Note that the body is plain text, not JSON, so a check that parses it as JSON fails on a healthy instance."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO NUMBER IN THE REPO. It is one compiled Haskell binary, which is far lighter than an interpreted stack, but it holds the whole tracked schema in memory as a schema cache and keeps a Postgres connection pool, so its footprint tracks the size of the user's schema rather than anything we can measure in advance. m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB) is the reasoned floor and keeps the deploy inside the no-card trial. Someone tracking hundreds of tables or running heavy subscriptions should expect to move to m1.mem16. Measure it on your run and write the number back rather than repeating this paragraph."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr, roughly GBP 33 a month; fits the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2', db_extensions:['pgcrypto'], port 8080, and env carrying HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET. ⚠️ plan_deploy will want to upsize a compose stack to m1.large once needs_compose is declared; pass flavor_id '3' explicitly to hold m1.medium. platform_facts: THE deploy VM RUNS DOCKER, NOT PODMAN. The compose project is named app-src, so containers are app-src-<service>-1 and volumes are app-src_<name>. Use `sudo docker ...` on the VM; podman is not installed. Several deploys rediscovered this independently.

SOURCE IS EITHER GIT OR UPLOAD, NEVER BOTH. For code that is not pushed, or is private, or needs fixing first: write the files locally, call prepare_upload, run the tar+curl block it returns, then pass the source_token and NO repo. ⚠️ prepare_upload EXCLUDES .env from the tarball by design, so secrets have to reach the VM another way (pass them to the deploy call, not in the tree).

A MANAGED DATABASE IS A SECOND VM WITH ITS OWN HOURLY RATE, and delete_deployment deliberately LEAVES IT BEHIND so your data survives the app. That means a teardown that stops at delete_deployment keeps billing a database nobody can reach. Call delete_database too, and say so to the user before either.

A MANAGED POSTGRES SERVES EXACTLY ONE DATABASE. pg_hba is evaluated before role privileges, so being superuser does not help. An app that wants a second database needs a second managed server. This has broken deploys that otherwise looked healthy.

get_deployment RETURNS THE MERGED redu.md ONLY WHEN IT FITS ITS RESPONSE BUDGET. Over budget - which is normal for a mature recipe or any large app - it withholds redu_md_markdown and returns redu_md_last_deploy_block plus redu_md_deploy_log_line instead. That is NOT an error and must not be retried: apply those two edits to the file on disk and change nothing else.

⛔ THE MERGE NEVER WRITES A NEW QUIRK. Whatever redu returns, it refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and nothing else. Every gotcha YOUR run discovered has to be typed into the quirks list by hand before you commit, or it is lost - and that list is the only part of the file that makes the next deploy cheaper.
⛔ NEVER WRITE A CREDENTIAL INTO redu.md. It is committed and read by the next person and the next agent. Names of variables, yes; their values, never. Hand secrets to the user in the session instead.

plan_deploy OVER-SIZES A PULLED COMPOSE STACK. Measured 8 times out of 8: declaring needs_compose makes it quote m1.large, roughly double the real requirement, because it cannot see that the images are pulled rather than built. Show the user the plan, but size from the app's real memory figure when you have one.

THE MANAGED DATABASE PASSWORD IS ON THE VM, NOT IN THE API. list_databases returns private_ip, port, db_name and db_user and DELIBERATELY NOT the password, so an agent that looks for it there finds nothing and starts guessing. The deploy writes the whole connection set into the compose project's .env on the app VM. Call get_env_keys for the NAMES first (no SSH, values never leave the VM); only if you need an actual VALUE, SSH in (get_ssh_command) and read that one key, `sudo grep '^PGPASSWORD=' /opt/app-src/.env`. ⚠️ That file is chmod 600 root:root so it needs sudo, and the database is on the PRIVATE network - reachable from the app VM, never from a laptop.

YOU CAN READ A DEPLOY VM WITHOUT SSHING INTO IT, and four tools do it: get_containers (what is running, health, restarts, crashed ones included), get_container_logs (what the app actually printed - the tool for 'deployed fine but does not work'), get_resource_usage (memory, disk, load, OOM kills) and get_env_keys (which variables got wired, by name). ⛔ get_instance_logs is the SERIAL CONSOLE and is not your app's logs; build_log stops when the build does. SSH is still yours for everything else - a shell on a real machine is the point, not a fallback. ⭐ MEASURED over 38 deploys: of 241 ssh escapes, 146 (61%) were exactly these four things, and the four tools were called 11 times. They are faster than a login, they cost the VM nothing extra (the reading is already cached), and reaching for ssh to run `docker ps` is the single most common wasted minute in a deploy.

⛔ THE PRIMARY SURFACE'S HOSTNAME COMES FROM THE TOP-LEVEL dname, NOT FROM expose[0].dname, WHICH IS SILENTLY DISCARDED. Extra expose entries DO keep the dname you give them, so the two behave differently and nothing tells you. If an app bakes its own public URL into config at boot (CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN, allowed_origins, SITE_URL), generate the full `<label>-<8 lowercase letters/digits>.redu.cloud` form yourself and pass it as the TOP-LEVEL dname, which is used verbatim. Passing it on expose[0] instead gets you an app configured for a hostname redu never created, answering 200 on a name it does not believe is its own.

WEBSOCKETS WORK THROUGH THE PROXY WITH NO CONFIGURATION: every proxy host redu creates has upgrade enabled. Measured at the protocol level, HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols with the subprotocol echoed back. ⚠️ TEST IT WITH `curl --http1.1`: plain curl negotiates HTTP/2, which has no Upgrade mechanism at all, so the app answers as an ordinary GET and the failure looks exactly like a proxy refusing to upgrade. Browsers use HTTP/1.1 for websockets regardless. Do not disable an app's realtime features on the strength of an HTTP/2 curl.

# Hasura GraphQL Engine v2 — single service.
#
# Derived from upstream install-manifests/docker-compose/docker-compose.yaml with:
#   - the bundled `postgres:15` service removed (redu provisions a managed Postgres
#     on its own private VM; DATABASE_URL is appended to this project's .env)
#   - the `data-connector-agent` service removed, along with the `depends_on` block
#     that named it and the HASURA_GRAPHQL_METADATA_DEFAULTS JSON that pointed at it
#   - dev mode and telemetry turned off, CORS narrowed, pg_dump API dropped
version: "3.6"

services:
  graphql-engine:
    image: hasura/graphql-engine:v2.50.0
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      # Managed Postgres on the private network. This one database both stores the
      # metadata (hdb_catalog schema) and is registered as the default GraphQL source.
      HASURA_GRAPHQL_DATABASE_URL: ${DATABASE_URL}

      # The entire access-control story of this app. Without it every anonymous
      # request resolves to the admin role.
      HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET: [REDACTED:value]}

      # Console on, served from the image instead of a CDN, behind the admin secret.
      HASURA_GRAPHQL_ENABLE_CONSOLE: "true"
      HASURA_GRAPHQL_CONSOLE_ASSETS_DIR: /srv/console-assets

      # Default also includes pgdump, an anonymous-by-default database dump endpoint.
      # metadata must stay in the list or the console stops being served.
      HASURA_GRAPHQL_ENABLED_APIS: graphql,metadata,config

      # Upstream's manifest sets dev mode true; it leaks internal error detail (SQL).
      HASURA_GRAPHQL_DEV_MODE: "false"
      # Defaults to enabled; anonymous usage reporting from server and console.
      HASURA_GRAPHQL_ENABLE_TELEMETRY: "false"
      # Default is allow-all.
      HASURA_GRAPHQL_CORS_DOMAIN: https://hasura-espcs2m5.redu.cloud

      HASURA_GRAPHQL_ENABLED_LOG_TYPES: startup, http-log, webhook-log, websocket-log, query-log
YAML
echo "--- written ---"
cat docker-compose.yml | head -5
ls -la

## Plan — Hasura GraphQL Engine v2 on redu

**What gets created (2 VMs):**

| Resource | Size | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| App VM — `hasura/graphql-engine:v2.50.0`, one container, port 8080 | m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB) | GBP 0.0278/hr |
| Managed Postgres, private network only, `pgcrypto` pre-created | m1.small (1 vCPU / 2 GB) | GBP 0.0174/hr |
| **Total** | | **GBP 0.0452/hr ≈ GBP 33/mo** |

Fits your quota (2/10 instances, 5/20 vCPU) and the no-card free trial. Billed hourly, deletable any time.

**URL:** `https://hasura-espcs2m5.redu.cloud` — generated up front so the CORS origin is wired to the real hostname rather than a name redu never created.

**Three things I changed from redu's generic plan:**

1. **Held m1.medium instead of the m1.large it quoted** (GBP 48/mo → 33/mo). It up-sizes every `needs_compose` stack assuming an on-VM build; this one pulls a prebuilt image and runs a single container. redu's own preflight flagged the disagreement with redu.md's record.
2. **`db_extensions: ["pgcrypto"]`** — Hasura's catalog init aborts on first boot if the app role can't create that extension. This is the one that would otherwise cost the deploy.
3. **`HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET` set** — a 48-char secret, generated and held locally. Upstream's default is *unset*, and unset means every anonymous request from the internet resolves to the **admin** role: read/write on every table plus the metadata API. Also dropped `pgdump` from the enabled APIs, turned off dev mode and telemetry, and narrowed CORS.

The compose file is one service — I removed upstream's bundled `postgres:15`, the `data-connector-agent`, its `depends_on` block, and the `METADATA_DEFAULTS` JSON that pointed at it.

**Shall I go ahead and deploy this?** Nothing is billed until you say yes.

  -X POST "https://$HOST/v1/graphql" \\
  -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)

# so the STATUS CODE cannot decide this. The BODY can: a served query has "data",

if grep -q '"data"' /tmp/hasura.anon && ! grep -q 'access-denied' /tmp/hasura.anon; then
  echo "FAIL: an ANONYMOUS GraphQL query was SERVED (HTTP $anon). The admin secret is not in effect."
  cat /tmp/hasura.anon

  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: anonymous query returned neither data nor an access-denied error:"
  cat /tmp/hasura.anon

  echo "FAIL: anonymous /v1/metadata answered $meta, expected 401."
  cat /tmp/hasura.meta
  exit 1
fi
echo "anonymous /v1/metadata: HTTP $meta (refused)"

The script judges the negative half by HTTP status, but `/v1/graphql` returns **200 with a GraphQL errors body** for access-denied; only `/v1/metadata` returns a real 401. I confirmed the secret is genuinely enforced from three independent angles before trusting it — the response body carries `access-denied` with no `data`, anonymous `/v1/metadata` is 401, and Hasura's own logs show the anonymous request as `level:error, request_mode:error` with no `user_vars`, next to the authenticated one stamped `x-hasura-role: admin`. An unsecured engine would have stamped the anonymous request admin too, so that last one settles it.

I fixed the script inside redu.md, then extracted it back out and ran it: it passes on the live instance and still fails loudly against a wrong secret.
